passages.text: Factors, including patient education, that impact cancer treatment adherence in low- and middle-income African countries: a scoping review
Purpose

Cancer-related morbidity and mortality are disproportionately higher in low- and middle-income countries. <sentence_start/>One factor that is crucial to improving outcomes is adherence to cancer treatments, which is lower in low- and middle-income countries, especially in Africa, due to patient, provider and system factors. <sentence_start/>This scoping review aims to map and summarise the characteristics of patient education strategies designed to improve cancer treatment adherence in low- and middle-income African countries.
Methods

This scoping review used the methods of the Joanna Briggs Institute framework. <sentence_start/>The review included English-language primary studies published in peer-reviewed journals. <sentence_start/>It focused on adults with cancer receiving an educational intervention aimed at improving treatment adherence in low- and middle-income African countries using narrative synthesis.
Results

Eleven included articles generated three overarching themes on treatment adherence: challenges of social structures; safe, meaningful patient education; and the power of interpersonal interactions between patients, healthcare professionals and families. <sentence_start/>Technology-assisted education, direct lectures, role playing and demonstration-based methods delivered through group and one-on-one sessions were effective strategies for improving treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>However, low-income and literacy, treatment complexity and lack of social support were frequently reported as barriers to improving cancer treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>Challenges of social structure in treatment adherence included low-literacy (and low-health literacy), cultural and religious beliefs, financial burdens, limited access to cancer care and inadequate health system infrastructure.
Conclusions

The mapped evidence highlights that there are several patient education strategies that have been published in low- and middle-income African countries. <sentence_start/>However, empirical evidence is limited, heterogeneous in findings and not evaluated with validated methods.
Introduction

Cancer is a global public health issue and the second leading cause of death after cardiovascular disease. <sentence_start/>In 2022, there were approximately 10 million cancer-related deaths worldwide, with low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) disproportionately higher, accounting for approximately 65% of these deaths [<citation rid="CR1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0140-6736(25)01635-6" pmid="41015051" pmcid="PMC12687902" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Cancer incidence is also rising globally [<citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3332/ecancer.2023.1594" pmcid="PMC10550290" pmid="37799947" count="1">2</citation>, <citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" count="1">3</citation>], largely because people are living longer [<citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" count="1">4</citation>] as other acute causes of death are managed more effectively. <sentence_start/>Ageing remains the greatest single risk factor for cancer [<citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MAJ.0000000000000281" pmid="24805784" pmcid="PMC4119927" count="1">5</citation>].

Cancer mortality is also higher in LMICs in Africa, accounting for around 7.8% of global cancer deaths in 2022 [<citation rid="CR6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3322/caac.21834" pmid="38572751" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adherence to cancer treatment refers to the degree to which a patient consistently follows their healthcare provider’s recommendations for cancer care [<citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Adherence rates to cancer treatment in LMICs in Africa are noted to be as low as 20% [<citation rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00289" pmid="36689700" pmcid="PMC10166491" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Key factors include poorer knowledge of causes of cancer, spiritual beliefs, financial challenges, weaker patient-provider relationships, inability to pay for treatment and fatalistic attitudes [<citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/oncol.2012.e5" pmid="25992207" pmcid="PMC4419635" count="1">9</citation>, <citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e09716" pmid="35770147" pmcid="PMC9234585" count="1">10</citation>].

Patient education is a structured, purposeful process through which health professionals provide individuals (and, where appropriate, families or carers) with information, skills and support to enhance their understanding of health conditions, treatments and self-care practices [<citation rid="CR11" ref-type="bibr" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This strategy is a highly effective approach in influencing treatment adherence in chronic diseases, including cancer [<citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2020.591610" pmcid="PMC7737519" pmid="33335858" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Well-designed education can enhance adherence, ease symptom burden, support lifestyle changes, improve quality of life and ultimately lower premature mortality [<citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4081/oncol.2012.e5" pmid="25992207" pmcid="PMC4419635" count="1">9</citation>, <citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e09716" pmid="35770147" pmcid="PMC9234585" count="1">10</citation>, <citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2021/8880366" pmcid="PMC8093042" pmid="33986806" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Educating patients and caregivers on diagnosis, treatment plans, self-administration of anti-cancer agents, potential side effects, non-pharmacological management, complications and the importance of attending clinic for all appointments has the potential to improve patient outcomes [<citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" count="1">15</citation>].

Beyond the African context targeted by this review, evidence from other global LMICs highlights that patient education has been shown to effectively improve health outcomes for oncology patients, including enhanced quality of life and reduced premature mortality [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.xcrm.2024.101517" pmid="38776876" pmcid="PMC11148561" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A 2023 review by Christiansen et al. [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>] found that technology-based interventions (especially interactive education videos) were the most frequently utilised and effective strategies, particularly for populations with low literacy, by enhancing cancer knowledge [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A 2022 systematic review by Chauke et al. reported that patient knowledge of disease and medication are one central mediating factor [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e09716" pmid="35770147" pmcid="PMC9234585" count="1">10</citation>], while Kostantinou et al. showed that digital education combining disease and medication information, motivational interviewing, reinforcement and motivational messages leads to improvements in treatment adherence [<citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33231691" doi="10.1093/tbm/ibaa118" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Such work requires consideration and understanding of literacy and health literacy in LMICs.

Most evidence in the context of LMICs has reported either on educational strategies [<citation rid="CR18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.31557/APJCP.2022.23.9.3035" pmid="36172666" pmcid="PMC9810294" count="1">18</citation>] or factors that influence cancer treatment adherence [<citation rid="CR19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ijmedinf.2021.104659" pmid="34929545" count="1">19</citation>], but not on the discrete context of the role of patient education on cancer treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>This is a gap in our knowledge of what constitutes successful patient education relative to improved cancer treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>Hence, this review builds on the recent reviews of Christiansen et al. [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>] and Chauke et al. [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e09716" pmid="35770147" pmcid="PMC9234585" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This scoping review aimed to map the literature on patient education specific to LMICs in Africa, with a particular focus on studies that identify cancer treatment adherence as a primary outcome.
Review questions
What are the characteristics of the content and mode of delivery of patient education that aim to improve cancer treatment adherence in LMICs in African countries?
What factors influence the success and implementation of patient education to improve cancer treatment adherence in LMICs in African countries?
Methods
The study protocols

This scoping review was guided by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews [<citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33038125" doi="10.11124/JBISRIR-D-19-00099" count="1">20</citation>] and the findings were reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) [<citation rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7326/M18-0850" pmid="30178033" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The protocol for this study is registered in the PROSPERO database under the registration ID 1021376.
Inclusion criteria
The focus of this scoping review was refined with the ‘population-concept-context’ mnemonic of the JBI methodology [<citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" count="1">22</citation>]:
Population

This scoping review considered studies conducted among adult (18 years or older) patients in LMICs in Africa (based on World Bank income classification, LMICs include low, lower middle and upper middle income), diagnosed with cancer (any type, any stage in the cancer continuum) and prescribed anti-cancer treatment (any kind) and peer-reviewed journals published in English.
Concepts
The concepts of interest for this review were related to:
I.

Patient education, including type of content (e.g. clinical, informational, psychological/emotional, social, spiritual), intervention(s) or strategies (e.g. tailored, general), delivery modes (e.g. technology-assisted/Short Message Service, video), and education method (e.g. 1:1 motivational interviewing, group education).
II.

Cancer treatment adherence including elements of social determinants of health (e.g. income and social protection, education, job (in)security and unemployment, working life conditions, food insecurity, housing, social inclusion, structural and social conflict, access to quality care) and other determinants (e.g. sex, religion, culture, health literacy, health system, healthcare provider).
Context

This review considered studies that reported on the implementation and evaluation of patient education, which had a primary outcome of, or focus on, cancer treatment adherence in inpatient or outpatient settings in LMICs in Africa.
Sources

This scoping review considered peer-reviewed publications in English. <sentence_start/>Studies using quantitative, qualitative and mixed-methods research designs were considered for inclusion. <sentence_start/>Eligible quantitative studies were experimental, observational or descriptive cross-sectional designs. <sentence_start/>Qualitative studies included in the review were interview or focus group designs, or qualitative descriptions of interventions. <sentence_start/>No restrictions were placed on the duration of follow-up. <sentence_start/>Studies were excluded if they did not focus on the two key concepts of interest: patient education or educational interventions, and cancer treatment adherence, including factors influential of adherence, as well as the grey literature.
Search strategy

An initial limited search of MEDLINE (PubMed) was undertaken to identify articles on the topic. <sentence_start/>The text words and key terms contained in the titles and abstracts of relevant articles, and the index terms used to describe the articles, were used to develop a full search strategy to be employed across all included databases. <sentence_start/>To enhance specificity and sensitivity, the ‘explode’ command, the truncation symbol (*), and Boolean terms (AND, OR) were used to combine the different key search concepts (patient self-management education; cancer treatment adherence; low- and middle-income Africa) (Table 1).

Four electronic databases were searched from their inception to March 2025, including the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE through PubMed, CINAHL and Web of Science. <sentence_start/>To identify unindexed articles in the searched databases, literature was searched using Google Scholar, as well as manual searches of reference lists of relevant articles in the field. <sentence_start/>Websites were also searched, including the World Health Organisation, Union for International Cancer Control, International Cancer Foundation, International Agency for Research on Cancer, American Cancer Society and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.
Study selection

All records were exported into EndNote software version 20.0 [<citation rid="CR23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5195/jmla.2021.1260" pmid="34629985" pmcid="PMC8485940" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Duplicates and documents assessed irrelevant with a ‘first pass’ rapid review by two authors (DTA and VNB) were removed.

Guided by the inclusion criteria, two authors (DTA and VNB) independently screened the full-text versions to determine the final number of included articles. <sentence_start/>Where there was reviewer disagreement between DTA and VNB, these authors met to discuss the study in question and together re-read the full-text version. <sentence_start/>The advice of the wider research team (DCC and PMD) helped to resolve any disagreements.
Methodological quality assessment

The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). <sentence_start/>The MMAT was selected because it provides criteria appraising studies with different methodological designs, including quantitative, qualitative and mixed-method studies. <sentence_start/>The two screening questions and five design-specific appraisal criteria were applied according to the methodological design of each included study [<citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" count="1">24</citation>].
Data extraction

Informed by the JBI data extraction template [<citation rid="CR22" ref-type="bibr" count="1">22</citation>] and our review questions, a data abstraction form, in Microsoft Excel format, was developed. <sentence_start/>Other information collected included geographic locations of studies, study settings and designs, research participants’ involvement and the interventions and strategies tested relative to cancer treatment adherence and education delivery modes. <sentence_start/>Any disagreements about data extracted were discussed between the two authors (DTA and VNB) and, when necessary, with the wider research team (DCC and PMD) until consensus was reached. <sentence_start/>Table 2 presents the data extraction form. <sentence_start/>Given the complexity of implementation studies and the heterogeneity in implementation components and study designs, appraisal of the quality of studies was not undertaken. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with other similarly designed systematic scoping reviews [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13643-019-0952-5" pmid="30704509" pmcid="PMC6354326" count="1">25</citation>].
Data analysis and narrative synthesis approach

Whilst there is a lack of consensus regarding the best approach for synthesising scoping review findings, narrative synthesis remains a recommended approach [<citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13643-019-0952-5" pmid="30704509" pmcid="PMC6354326" count="1">25</citation>] including within the JBI literature review methodology [<citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11124/JBIES-20-00364" pmid="33989268" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This is an approach to the synthesis of evidence relevant to a wide range of issues [<citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>] by using words and text to ‘tell the story’, that is, to summarise and explain the results of several investigations [<citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this review, tabulation, textual descriptions and thematic analysis utilising concept mapping, as suggested by Popay et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>], were employed iteratively by the research team.
Results
Search results

A total of 3785 studies were obtained through database retrieval and reference tracing. <sentence_start/>After removal of duplicates and documents assessed as irrelevant with a ‘first pass’ rapid review, 251 articles underwent title and abstract screening. <sentence_start/>This process further excluded 222 articles, reducing the number of eligible articles for full-text review to 29. <sentence_start/>Of the 29 full-text articles assessed for eligibility, 11 articles were included to comply with the inclusion criteria (Fig. 1).Fig. 1
PRISMA flowchart
Characteristics of included studies

Among the 11 included studies (Table 3): three were conducted in Ethiopia [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>-<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" count="1">31</citation>]; two in Tanzania [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajog.2020.07.018" pmid="32682861" count="1">32</citation>, <citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>]; three in Kenya [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>-<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>] and one each in Malawi [<citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>], Rwanda [<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>], South Africa and Uganda [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The majority of the studies was published after 2018 [<citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>-<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>], with two studies published between 2012 and 2016 [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0166411" pmid="27851785" pmcid="PMC5112982" count="1">40</citation>], and one study published before 2010 [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>].

The 11 studies included a total of 3246 participants, the majority of whom had cervical cancer, followed by breast cancer (this was because some of the included studies focused exclusively on breast and cervical cancer). <sentence_start/>The participant sample sizes ranged from 40 to 825 participants. <sentence_start/>The mean ages ranged from 18 to 66 years. <sentence_start/>All 11 studies included people with cancer across all stages, cancer types and treatment phases.

There were six experimental studies [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajog.2020.07.018" pmid="32682861" count="1">32</citation>-<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>-<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>], two qualitative studies [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>] and three observational studies [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>-<citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most of the studies employed a quantitative design, while two [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>] were purely qualitative, and one experimental study [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>] adopted a mixed-methods design that included a qualitative component. <sentence_start/>Of the experimental studies, two were randomised controlled trials (RCTs) [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>], while the remaining four used a pre- and post-test design [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajog.2020.07.018" pmid="32682861" count="1">32</citation>, <citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>All experimental studies, including the mixed methods design which incorporated a qualitative design, were Methodological quality assessment

All included studies met the two MMAT screening criteria, with none receiving a response of ‘no’ or ‘can’t tell’. <sentence_start/>This indicates that all studies had clearly defined research questions and that collected data were considered appropriate for addressing their research objectives. <sentence_start/>The other five criteria were based on the study design and were used to assess the methodological quality of the included studies. <sentence_start/>Qualitative studies generally meet all MMAT criteria. <sentence_start/>Quantitative descriptive studies (observational studies) also demonstrated good methodological quality; however, two studies [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" count="1">31</citation>] were assessed as ‘can’t tell’ regarding whether their samples were representative of the target population, as both studies were conducted in a single hospital. <sentence_start/>Quantitative non-randomized intervention studies had some methodological limitations, including unclear reporting of participant representativeness [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>, <citation rid="CR41" ref-type="bibr" count="1">41</citation>], lack of adjustment for potential confounding factors [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>] and unclear reporting of completeness of outcome data [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>] (Table 4).
Responding to the review questions
Education methods included:

direct lecture, role playing and demonstration (<italic>n</italic> = 2 studies) [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>];

group education sessions facilitated by a researcher or healthcare professional (<italic>n</italic> = 4 studies) [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajog.2020.07.018" pmid="32682861" count="1">32</citation>, <citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>];
1:1 education sessions using motivational interviewing (<italic>n</italic> = 2 studies) [36,; or

a combination of group education, either preceded or followed by a 1:1 session (<italic>n</italic> = 1 study) [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>].

The intensity or duration of education ranged from 2 days to 5 months, with only one study reporting an intervention of five months’ duration [<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most studies ranged from minutes to 3 weeks of intervention duration [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajog.2020.07.018" pmid="32682861" count="1">32</citation>-<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>].
The delivery modes of patient education reported in the studies included in this review focused largely on technology-assisted interventions or strategies, such as:
internet-based support interventions (<italic>n</italic> = 2 studies) [34,;
videos (<italic>n</italic> = 2 studies) [32, and

a full-process information management system (<italic>n</italic> = 1 study) [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>].
Characteristics of patient education to improve treatment adherence in LMICs in Africa

The content of patient education interventions and strategies reported in the literature, contextual to LMICs in Africa, is varied, including information support about tumour-specific disease and treatment knowledge, available aid resources or organisational service information, outpatient consultation arrangements and public lectures [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>-<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>].

Nurses were the most frequent patient education provider (<italic>n</italic> = 3 studies) [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>], followed by allied healthcare professionals (<italic>n</italic> = 2 studies) [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Three studies reported the researcher (master’s degree holders) as the role to facilitate patient education [<citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajog.2020.07.018" pmid="32682861" count="1">32</citation>-<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>].

Qualitative studies utilised one-on-one semi-structured interviews of varying duration [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>] to assess barriers and facilitators [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>] and also to evaluate programme effectiveness [<citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s13187-018-1437-2" pmid="30368651" pmcid="PMC6920575" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Observational studies employed cross-sectional designs to explore factors and behaviours influencing cancer treatment adherence [<citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="CR31" ref-type="bibr" count="1">31</citation>].
Factors influencing the implementation and uptake of patient education in LMICs in Africa

Multiple and often competing factors influenced the success of patient education for adults undergoing cancer treatment in LMICs in Africa [<citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1547-5069.2012.01444.x" pmid="22551013" pmcid="PMC3366425" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Individuals with higher levels of income, for instance, reported better access to different anti-cancer and supportive care medications and resources necessary for effective cancer management [<citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fpubh.2021.628744" pmid="33996712" pmcid="PMC8120029" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, patients with higher education levels appear to have better understandings of their cancer condition and treatment options, are more informed in their decision-making and report more effective day-to-day management [<citation rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-024-54444-2" pmid="39557933" pmcid="PMC11574020" count="1">44</citation>].
Narrative synthesised findings

Relative to each review question, key concepts supported by textual description were constructed through the qualitative analytical approach, with an overarching theme derived. <sentence_start/>Table 5 presents the analytical findings.
Discussion

This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on factors including patient education that impact cancer treatment adherence in LMICs in Africa. <sentence_start/>The review identified three overarching themes: (1) safe and meaningful patient education, (2) challenges of social structures and (3) the power of interpersonal interactions among people living with cancer, healthcare professionals and family caregivers. <sentence_start/>These findings reveal that improving treatment adherence requires more than changing individual patient behaviour.
Patient education to improve cancer patient treatment, understanding and adherence

In LMICs, several studies that have explored cancer treatment adherence highlight health education as a key approach to improving adherence [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For instance, a study conducted in Ethiopia [<citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>] suggested the importance of improving patients’ understanding of their illness and treatment through health education programmes; however, the authors did not specify content or what type of educational approach would be most suitable in this context. <sentence_start/>Yates et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2020.591610" pmcid="PMC7737519" pmid="33335858" count="1">12</citation>] and Brunelli [<citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" count="1">45</citation>] emphasise that patient education, an active and participatory process, plays a crucial role in improving health outcomes among people with cancer and chronic diseases, as long as the education delivered is personalised and tailored to the context and situatedness of the patient and their support people. <sentence_start/>Some studies from LMICs support this view, underscoring the need for standardised yet tailored patient education, though they stop short of making explicit what might comprise appropriately tailored education [<citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>].

Research by Lidofsky et al<italic>.</italic> and Howell et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00520-016-3500-z" pmid="28058570" count="1">46</citation>] align with the positions of Yates et al. [<citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fonc.2020.591610" pmcid="PMC7737519" pmid="33335858" count="1">12</citation>] and Bruneli [<citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" count="1">45</citation>], concluding that tailored patient education programmes are associated with improved adherence, which, in turn, enhances cancer outcomes and other health-related outcomes, such as quality of life [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00520-016-3500-z" pmid="28058570" count="1">46</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Moreover, such programmes not only empower people affected by cancer by increasing their knowledge about the disease and its treatment, but also enhance the capacity of health care professionals in delivering more effective person-centred care [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0109788" pmid="25333793" pmcid="PMC4198132" count="1">47</citation>].

A variety of patient education intervention delivery modes have been utilised in LMICs. <sentence_start/>A 2024 study in Kenya that aimed to improve patients’ understanding of treatment recommendations evaluated the effectiveness of short message service support and found that this delivery mode intervention significantly enhanced treatment adherence [<citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>].

Christiansen et al. [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>], in their systematic review, on the other hand, revealed that technology-based interventions, particularly interactive video-based learning, were among the most common and effective education methods. <sentence_start/>They stated that visual components are especially valuable in populations with limited literacy, which is a prevalent issue in LMICs. <sentence_start/>Such approaches not only improve patients’ knowledge but also help them engage with information that aligns with their needs and preferences [<citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac206" pmid="36269170" pmcid="PMC9847564" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This is important in rural areas where lower education levels and poor literacy and health literacy often contribute to misconceptions about cancer, poor perceptions of treatment and difficulties in understanding complex medical conditions [<citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.21.00315" pmid="35175832" pmcid="PMC8863121" count="1">37</citation>, <citation rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33604453" pmcid="PMC7889072" count="1">48</citation>].

Kostantinou et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="33231691" doi="10.1093/tbm/ibaa118" count="1">17</citation>] reported that motivational interviewing, regular reinforcement and motivational messages, as methods to deliver patient education, lead to improvements in treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>Similarly, Chauke et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e09716" pmid="35770147" pmcid="PMC9234585" count="1">10</citation>] supported these strategies but noted that their success largely depends on addressing literacy barriers and communication challenges within LMICs, as well as on developing policies that facilitate effective patient-provider communication. <sentence_start/>To address these challenges, educational materials should be both culturally sensitive and standardised, while allowing for adaptation to the local contexts.
The power of interpersonal interactions between patients, healthcare professionals and family on cancer treatment adherence

Relationships among healthcare professionals, people living with cancer and family caregivers play a critical role in effective cancer care. <sentence_start/>Moreover, active engagement and communication between these groups is integral in facilitating the abilities of individuals with cancer to manage, thereby improving the likelihood of treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>Several studies [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4236/ojn.2024.143007" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.apjon.2022.01.012" pmid="35136829" pmcid="PMC8813188" count="1">49</citation>] highlight that strong interpersonal communication and collaboration among these stakeholder groups help patients better understand their illness, recognise the importance of adhering to treatment and anticipate potential side effects. <sentence_start/>Research by Selman et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>] and Habimana et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>] demonstrated that effective communication between patients, family caregivers and healthcare providers improves trust, shared understanding and emotional support, all of which serve to positively influence cancer treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with evidence from high-income countries, where quality interactions have been shown to improve cancer care outcomes [<citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.soncn.2018.06.007" pmcid="PMC6156926" pmid="30100368" count="1">50</citation>-<citation rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3332/ecancer.2019.944" pmcid="PMC6722106" pmid="31552117" count="1">52</citation>].

However, in LMICs in Africa, several challenges hinder the development of such meaningful interactions. <sentence_start/>These include limited knowledge of cancer care among healthcare professionals, including negative perceptions about treatment options, efficacy and outcomes and socio-cultural factors that constrain the delivery of effective patient and family education [<citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3332/ecancer.2019.944" pmcid="PMC6722106" pmid="31552117" count="1">52</citation>, <citation rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3332/ecancer.2021.1209" pmcid="PMC8057781" pmid="33912234" count="1">53</citation>]. <sentence_start/>McMahon et al<italic>.</italic> [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>] also noted that many individuals living with cancer in LMICs in Africa often perceive cancer as an incurable condition, which undermines motivation for treatment commencement, let alone adherence. <sentence_start/>Similarly, family caregivers can have insufficient understanding of cancer treatments, hold unfavourable attitudes towards medical care and, sometimes, adhere to religious or cultural beliefs that weaken confidence in medical interventions [<citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>, <citation rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12905-020-00908-8" pmcid="PMC7065362" pmid="32160874" count="1">54</citation>].

To address these challenges, evidence from LMICs in Africa consistently emphasises the importance of culturally sensitive and contextually appropriate patient education programmes [<citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5334/aogh.2503" pmid="31673514" pmcid="PMC6798900" count="1">33</citation>, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31283411" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00118" pmcid="PMC6690653" count="1">38</citation>, <citation rid="CR55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3332/ecancer.2019.942" pmcid="PMC6722105" pmid="31552115" count="1">55</citation>, <citation rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15430/JCP.2019.24.1.33" pmid="30993093" pmcid="PMC6453587" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Such programmes can strengthen the cooperation between patients, family caregivers and healthcare professionals by improving communication, trust and shared responsibility in care. <sentence_start/>Further exploration of cancer treatment experience that involves diverse stakeholders is vital.
The challenge of social structures on cancer treatment initiation and adherence in LMICs in Africa

Factors influencing cancer treatment initiation and adherence in LMICs in Africa are multifaceted and often intersect, including literacy, cultural and religious beliefs, economic burden, healthcare access (such as distance to health facilities) and health system infrastructure challenges [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmj.b1326" pmid="19386672" pmcid="PMC3273778" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These are explained in greater depth below:
Literacy

Literacy is the ability to identify, understand, interpret, create and communicate using written materials [<citation rid="CR57" ref-type="bibr" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Health literacy, which is a component of literacy, is the ability of individuals to understand and use health-related information in ways that promote and maintain good health [<citation rid="CR58" ref-type="bibr" count="1">58</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Digital literacy also refers to the ability to use technologies to access, evaluate and communicate information [<citation rid="CR59" ref-type="bibr" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In many African countries, low health literacy hinders patients’ understanding of cancer, its treatment and the importance of adhering to treatment, fostering myths that cancer is incurable [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>] and undermining informed decision-making [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These misconceptions contribute to reduced adherence, with some patients discontinuing treatment after it has begun [<citation rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15430/JCP.2019.24.1.33" pmid="30993093" pmcid="PMC6453587" count="1">56</citation>, <citation rid="CR60" ref-type="bibr" count="1">60</citation>, <citation rid="CR61" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph18020618" pmid="33450864" pmcid="PMC7828302" count="1">61</citation>].
Cultural and religious beliefs

In LMICs in Africa, cultural and religious beliefs strongly shape how cancer patients view their illness, treatment and healthcare choices. <sentence_start/>Traditional medicine and spiritual practices often take precedence over modern evidence-based medical care, leading some patients to delay, discontinue or forgo cancer treatment in favour of alternative therapies such as holy water or traditional healers [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>], which can worsen outcomes [<citation rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15430/JCP.2019.24.1.33" pmid="30993093" pmcid="PMC6453587" count="1">56</citation>, <citation rid="CR62" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1136/bmjopen-2022-071406" pmid="37643843" pmcid="PMC10465914" count="1">62</citation>-<citation rid="CR64" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1200/GO.23.00148" pmid="37992269" pmcid="PMC10681531" count="1">64</citation>].
Economic burden

In LMICs in Africa, the financial burden of cancer severely limits access to and continuity of treatment [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>]. <sentence_start/>High cost for care, medications, transport and lost wages, often compounded by lack of health insurance, create major barriers [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>], leading many to seek financial help through social media, while others face these challenges without external support [<citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31834831" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00129" pmcid="PMC6939739" count="1">65</citation>-<citation rid="CR68" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/oncolo/oyac127" pmid="35791963" pmcid="PMC9632304" count="1">68</citation>].
Healthcare access and health system infrastructure challenges

In LMICs in Africa, gaps in healthcare access and health system infrastructure hinder cancer treatment initiation and adherence. <sentence_start/>The limited or absence of facilities, shortages of trained oncology staff, poor transport in rural areas, overcrowding, long waiting times and limited specialised oncology services in urban settings all create significant barriers to care [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR56" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15430/JCP.2019.24.1.33" pmid="30993093" pmcid="PMC6453587" count="1">56</citation>, <citation rid="CR65" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31834831" doi="10.1200/JGO.19.00129" pmcid="PMC6939739" count="1">65</citation>].

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that treatment initiation and adherence are shaped by interconnected social and structural factors rather than by individual patient behaviour alone [<citation rid="CR69" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11606-021-06648-1" pmid="33660211" pmcid="PMC8390603" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While the existing literature widely acknowledges that adherence is governed by this complex interaction of socioeconomic, cultural and structural factors [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>, <citation rid="CR70" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.canep.2014.03.012" pmid="24768601" count="1">70</citation>], these studies suffer from both notable heterogeneity and methodological limitations. <sentence_start/>Primarily, prior research has relied on divergent measurement tools and evaluated outcomes almost from the patient’s perspective only. <sentence_start/>In addition, the methodological quality appraisal indicated that although most included studies were of generally good methodological quality, some non-randomised studies had limitations related to participant representativeness, adjustment for confounding factors and completeness of outcome data.

Studies in Ethiopia (2015; 2023), for example, employed a cross-sectional design and self-administered questionnaires targeting only people living with cancer in a hospital setting [<citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" count="1">29</citation>, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/10732748231185010" pmcid="PMC10557419" pmid="37795961" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The key factors identified in this study were related primarily to sociocultural related to sociocultural influence. <sentence_start/>A study conducted in Kenya [<citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s13027-022-00444-0" pmcid="PMC9258164" pmid="35794634" count="1">35</citation>] employed a qualitative study design, focused solely on patients and identified several barriers to adherence, including lack of financial means, difficulty with the convenience of appointments, such as distance to facility, appointment times, long lines, limited appointments and lack of proper or sufficient information about chemotherapy. <sentence_start/>Notably, this study excluded other important stakeholders, such as family caregivers and health care professionals, whose perspectives might have contributed to a more comprehensive understanding of the issue.

These findings are consistent with the literature from LMICs beyond Africa [<citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.heliyon.2022.e09716" pmid="35770147" pmcid="PMC9234585" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Studies conducted in other LMICs have similarly reported that poor treatment adherence is influenced by a combination of lack of knowledge about cancer and its treatment, negative attitude towards cancer care, limited access and cultural and religious beliefs. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that the factors to treatment adherence identified in this review are not unique to African settings but are common across many resource-constrained settings. <sentence_start/>In sharp contrast, studies from high-income countries report that although socioeconomic inequalities remain important, patients benefit from stronger health systems, more comprehensive insurance coverage and greater availability of patient education and supportive care services which may help improve treatment adherence [<citation rid="CR71" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12913-024-11129-2" pmid="38807237" pmcid="PMC11134650" count="1">71</citation>].
Limitations of the study

This scoping review is subject to several limitations including (1) limited number of available articles addressing patient education and cancer treatment adherence in LMCs in Africa, limiting the comprehensiveness of findings, (2) methodological differences in the included studies, such as different study objectives and outcome measures which complicate the ability to draw uniform conclusions, (3) the inclusion of English-only studies and exclusion of grey literature may have resulted in the omission of relevant articles and (4) most studies lacked long-term data and standardised tools to measure treatment adherence, limiting insights into the effectiveness of patient education. <sentence_start/>Addressing these gaps in future research will be important to developing a more comprehensive understanding of the role of patient education in improving cancer treatment adherence in African LMICs. <sentence_start/>In addition, this review does not include individuals who do not access cancer care, a population about which little is currently known.
Implications for research

In LMICs in Africa, patient education arguably represents a critical role in improving cancer treatment adherence and outcomes for people with cancer. <sentence_start/>However, the most effective educational approach to improve cancer treatment adherence among the African population is unclear. <sentence_start/>Future research should consider context-specific, evidence-based, tailored educational interventions developed in collaboration with African people with cancer. <sentence_start/>Educational interventions should be co-designed, including diverse stakeholder groups, specifically people with cancer, family caregivers and healthcare professionals. <sentence_start/>Studies must aim to confirm or refute previously identified factors to develop a comprehensive understanding of cancer treatment adherence. <sentence_start/>To this end, longitudinal studies will be necessary to determine the efficacy of patient education programmes on cancer treatment adherence and longer-term health-related outcomes, for instance, quality of life.
Conclusion

The mapped evidence highlights that patient education is frequently used and associated with the potential for improving cancer treatment adherence in the African region. <sentence_start/>However, treatment adherence is influenced by multiple interconnected factors, such as limited health literacy and cultural and religious beliefs. <sentence_start/>The review also highlighted that the success of patient education intervention is also shaped by factors such as effective patient-provider communication and literacy level. <sentence_start/>Despite the potential, empirical evidence is limited, and the available evidence is heterogeneous in its objectives, design and outcomes. <sentence_start/>This methodological heterogeneity hinders a comprehensive understanding of the content, modes and methods of education delivery required to affect cancer treatment adherence, underscoring the need for further research.
